1.17.m: Bhīṣma said: / "What wonder occurred then at that sacrifice, O best of the twice-born? / How did Rudra remain there, and Viṣṇu too, the foremost of the gods?
What was done there by Gāyatrī, who stood in the role of wife? / And what was done by the Ābhīras, who know righteous conduct, when they found out, O sage?
Relate this account to me as it happened, just as it was done / by the Ābhīras and by Brahmā; this is a great wonder to me."
Pulastya said: / "Whatever wondrous event took place at that sacrifice, O ruler of men, / I shall relate all of that; listen with a single mind, O king!"
Rudra, however, having entered the assembly, performed a great marvel; / assuming a contemptible form, the god came there near the twice-born.
Viṣṇu did not do anything, because he stood in pre-eminence. / But the cowherd boys, having learned of the disappearance of the cowherd girl,
and likewise all those cowherd women, came into the presence of Brahmā, / seeing her bound with a girdle, standing at the boundary of the sacrifice.
“Alas, daughter!” cried the mother then, and the father: “Alas, little daughter!” / “O sister!” cried all the relatives, and her friends with friendliness: “Alas, friend!
By whom were you brought here, beautiful girl marked with red lac? / Having removed your sari, by whom was a woollen garment put on [you]?
And by whom, daughter, was this matted hair bound with red thread?” / Hearing such words, Hari himself spoke:
“She was brought here by us and appointed as a wife; / the maiden has been taken by Brahmā. Do not lament here!
She is meritorious, fortunate, and the delighter of the family of all. / If she were not meritorious, how could she come to the assembly?
Knowing this, O fortunate one, you ought not to grieve; / this highly fortunate maiden of yours has obtained the god Viriñcana.
Yogins endowed with yoga, and Brahmins who have reached the further shore of the Vedas, / do not attain, even praying for it, that state which your daughter has attained.
Knowing you to be righteous, of good conduct, and affectionate toward dharma, / this maiden was then given by me to Viriñci.
Saved by her, go to the divine, magnificent realms! / And in your family, for the sake of accomplishing the work of the gods,
I shall make an incarnation; indeed, that will be my sport. / When Nanda and the others on the surface of the earth
make an incarnation, then I too will dwell in their midst. / All your daughters will dwell together with me.
There will be no fault in that, neither hatred nor envy; / then the cowherds and men will make no fear.
And no fault will ever accrue to her by this act.” / Hearing the words of Viṣṇu, they bowed down and then departed.
[They said:] “Thus this boon, O god, which has been given, will indeed come to pass for me: / that an incarnation, an instrument of dharma, is to be made in our family.
From the very sight of you we become dwellers of heaven; / and this auspicious maiden is a savior of me along with my families.”
[They said:] “So be it, O Lord of gods! May this grant of boons be yours, O all-pervading one!” / The cowherds were then conciliated by the god Viṣṇu himself.
By Brahmā too, indeed, it was spoken thus with his left hand. / But the fair-complexioned girl was filled with shame at the sight of her relatives:
“By whom was I told of, so that they came to this region?” / Then, seeing them, the cowherd maiden Gāyatrī spoke,
with her left hand [raised] toward all of them, preceded by an obeisance: / “I am staying here, mother, having approached Brahmā.
I have obtained as husband the god who is the origin of everything, the lord of the universe; / I am not to be lamented by you, nor by father, nor by relatives.
Let my band of friends depart, and sisters along with children; / my welfare should be reported to all; I remain with the deities.”
When they had all departed, that slender-waisted Gāyatrī / shone together with Brahmā, having entered the sacrificial enclosure as a faithful wife.
Brahmā was begged by the Brahmins: “Grant us our desired boons!” / Then Brahmā also gave them the boon they desired,
and that which was given was approved by that goddess Gāyatrī. / That virtuous woman remained in the sacrifice, standing near the deities.
Then that sacrifice advanced for a full divine hundred years. / But the one with matted hair approached the sacrificial enclosure for the sake of alms,
holding a large skull, adorned with five severed heads; / standing at a distance, he was loathed by the sacrificial priests and the assembly members:
“How have you arrived here, condemned by the expounders of the Veda?” / Even while being thus driven away and reviled by those twice-born,
Maheśvara, having smiled, said to all those twice-born: / “Here in the sacrifice of the grandfather, which gives satisfaction to all,
no one is driven away at all, except me, O best of the twice-born!” / The one with matted hair was then told by them: “Eat food, and then go!”
And by the one with matted hair they were told: “Having eaten, I will go, O twice-born!” / Having spoken thus, he sat down, placing the skull in front.
Observing their deed, the Lord devised a crooked trick: / having left the skull on the ground, looking at those twice-born,
he said: “I am going to Puṣkara for a bath, O best of the twice-born.” / Told by them, “Go quickly!”, the Supreme Lord went away.
Remaining in the sky, having bewildered the dwellers of heaven out of curiosity, / when the one with matted hair had gone to Puṣkara for a bath, the twice-born [said]:
“How can an oblation be performed here while a skull remains in the assembly? / Formerly Prajāpati declared that skull-ends are impure.”
One Brahmin in the assembly said: “I will cast away the skull.” / It was lifted by the assembly member and thrown away with his own hand.
Just as quickly another remained there; it was lifted up yet again; / so a second, a third, twenty, even thirty, alas!
And fifty, and a hundred, a thousand, and ten thousand; / in this way, no end of the skulls could be reached by the best of the twice-born.
Having bowed to the god with matted hair, they approached him for refuge, / reaching the forest of Puṣkara, and intensely with Vedic prayers
they praised him all together; then Hara himself was pleased. / Thereupon Śiva gave a vision to the twice-born on account of their devotion.
Then the god said to those excellent twice-born bowed with devotion: / “The production of the sacrificial cake cannot occur without a potsherd.
Comply with my word, O Brahmins: let there be the Sviṣṭakṛt portion for me. / When this is done, all is accomplished; let this be my command.”
“So be it,” said the twice-born to Śambhu, “we shall indeed carry out your command.” / The Lord, skull in hand, said to the divine Grandfather:
“Choose a boon, O Brahmā, whatever lies dear in your heart! / I will grant you everything; there is nothing not to be given by me, O lord.”
Brahmā said: / “I will not take a boon from you; I am consecrated, seated in the assembly; / and I am the granter of all desires to whoever petitions me here.”
To the Grandfather speaking thus, the giver of boons in that sacrifice, / Rudra said, “So be it,” and asked for a boon from him.
Then, after a manvantara had elapsed, the Lord himself once again / made the place Brahmottara, the god Śambhu himself.
He who had attained complete mastery even in the four Vedas, / at that time, then, the god, for the sight of the city
and conversation with the twice-born, went to the assembly out of curiosity. / In that very guise of a madman, while the sacrificial remnants were being offered, Maheśvara
entered the abode of Brahmā, seen by the gods and best of the twice-born. / Some laughed at him, and some reviled him;
other twice-born sprinkled that madman with dust; / and others, strong and arrogant with power, [struck him] with clods and clubs;
striking him, they made a mocking clapping of hands. / Then other young religious students there, seizing his matted locks, nearby
asked about that observance of his vows: “By whom was this shown to you? / Here there are beautiful women; have you come for their sake?”

"By which teacher, a beholder of sin, was this conduct shown to you,
by which, speaking like a madman, you run around in our midst?

My phallus is the form of Brahmā, and Janārdana is the vulva.
This seed is being sown; yet the world torments [itself] otherwise.

This son was engendered by me, and by him I was engendered.
For the sake of Mahādeva the creation was created, and his wife in the Himālaya.

Umā was given to Rudra; say, whose daughter is she?
You are fools, you know nothing; let the Lord speak to you."

"This conduct was not performed by Brahmā, nor was it ever shown by Viṣṇu,
nor even by the god Giriśa, though he committed the murder of a Brahmin.

Why do you revile the god? You are surely to be killed by us today!"
Being struck thus by the Brahmins there, Śaṅkara,

smiling, said to all the Brahmins, O best of kings:
"Do you not know me, O Brahmins, [taking me to be] a madman whose senses are lost?

You are all compassionate, established in friendship,
[yet you strike] Hara who bears this disguise, who holds the form of Brahman while speaking."

Deluded by the illusory power of that god, those best of Brahmins
struck the wearer of matted hair with their hands, feet, and fists,

and also with sticks and pegs, him who wore the guise of a madman.
Being afflicted by those Brahmins, he then fell into anger.

Then they were cursed by the god: "May you be bereft of the Vedas,
with erect matted hair, fallen from sacrifices, consorting with other men's wives,

delighting in prostitutes and gambling, bereft of fathers and mothers!
No son will inherit ancestral wealth or Vedic learning.

May they all be deluded, deprived of all their senses,
eating the dreadful food of beggars, living on balls of rice given by others,

maintaining themselves, devoid of possessiveness, abandoned by dharma!
However, those Brahmins by whom compassion was bestowed upon me when I was mad now,

theirs shall be wealth and sons, female and male slaves, goats and sheep;
and women born of noble families shall be theirs in this world, since I am pleased!"

Having thus given a curse and a boon, the Lord disappeared.
When the god was gone, the Brahmins, realizing he was the Lord Śaṅkara,

though searching diligently, when they did not see him,
then, observing vows, came to the forest of Puṣkara.

Having bathed in Jyeṣṭhasaras, the Brahmins muttered the Śatarudriya.
At the end of their recitation, the god spoke to them with a bodiless voice:

"An untruth has never been spoken by me even in jest, how much less [now]?
Since punishment has befallen you, I shall grant you well-being once more.

Those Brahmins who are calm, self-controlled, devoted, and steadfast in me,
their Veda is not cut off, nor their wealth, nor their offspring.

Those who are devoted to the fire-offering, devoted to Janārdana,
and who worship Brahmā and the sun, the mass of radiance,

no misfortune exists for them whose minds are established in equanimity."
Having spoken words to this extent, he became silent.

Having obtained the boon and grace from Maheśvara, the god of gods,
they all went together to where the god, the Grandfather, was.

Standing before Viriñci, pleasing him with the recitation of Saṃhitās,
Brahmā, being pleased, said to them: "Let a boon be chosen from me as well."

At that word of Brahmā, all the best of Brahmins were delighted:
"What boon should be asked, O Brahmins, when the Grandfather is well pleased?

May the agnihotras, the Vedas, the various scriptures,
and the realms endowed with offspring be ours by the granting of this boon!"

While they were thus talking among themselves there, anger entered the Brahmins:
"Who are you? Who are the prominent ones here? We are the best!" and so said the others.

"No, no!" [said] the Brahmins to those twice-born assembled there.
Looking at the Brahmins filled with anger, Brahmā said:

"Since you stood outside the assembly in three groups,
therefore let there be one root-dwelling company for you, O twice-born.

Those who stood neutral, let them become indifferent.
Those who stood equipped with weapons, wearing unsheathed swords, desiring to fight,

let a third group be called Kauśika, O twice-born.
This place, arranged in three ways, shall entirely belong to you.

Here, those spoken of from without by the word 'people' are the subjects.
This place cannot be easily known; Viṣṇu will surely protect it.

Given by me, it will be long-lasting and indestructible."
Having spoken thus, Brahmā then looked toward that conclusion.

Those Brahmins gathered together, filled with anger and impatience,
feeding guests and devoted to the study of the Veda,

[remained in] this supreme sacred site named Puṣkara, belonging to Brahmā.
The peaceful Brahmins who reside there dwell as inhabitants of the sacred site.

Nothing will be difficult for them to attain in the world of Brahmā.
At Kokāmukha, Kurukṣetra, Naimiṣa, the gathering of sages,

in Vārāṇasī, Prabhāsa, and likewise at Badarikāśrama,
at Gaṅgādvāra, Prayāga, and the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean,

at Rudrakoṭi, Virūpākṣa, and likewise in the forest of Mitra—
at all these holy places, the accomplishment that requires twelve years

is obtained by men in this world in six months, O best of kings,
at Puṣkara, without doubt, if there is practice of celibacy.

It is the supreme among holy places and the best among sacred sites,
always worshipped by the venerable, endowed with devotion to the Grandfather.

Beyond this, I shall recount the great debate that occurred
between Sāvitrī and Brahmā, which was made in jest.

At the departure of Sāvitrī, all the wives of the gods arrived.
The renowned wife of Viṣṇu, born to Khyāti from Bhṛgu,

the ever-invited Lakṣmī, came there in haste;
and the illustrious Madirā, Yoganidrā who bestows prosperity,

Śrī whose abode is the lotus, Bhūti, Kīrti, wise Śraddhā,
Puṣṭi, and Tuṣṭi—these goddesses came, having assembled.

Satī, the daughter of Dakṣa, the auspicious Pārvatī called Umā,
the goddess who is the beauty of the three worlds, granter of good fortune to women,

Jayā and Vijayā, Madhucchandā, Amarāvatī,
Supriyā, and Janakāntā [came] to the auspicious abode of Sāvitrī.

They arrived together with Gaurī, adorned with beautiful garments and ornaments;
and the daughter of Puloman, Śakrāṇī, along with the Apsarases,

Svāhā and Svadhā arrived, and beautiful-faced Dhūmorṇā;
and Yakṣī, Rākṣasī, and Gaurī of great wealth,

Manojavā, wife of Vāyu, and Ṛddhi, beloved of the giver of wealth;
the divine maidens arrived thus, and the Dānavī women, beloved of the Danus,

the great wives of the seven sages, and the excellent women of the seers;
likewise sisters, daughters, and hosts of Vidyādharīs,

Rākṣasīs, daughters of the ancestors, and other mothers of the world.
With her brides and daughters-in-law, Sāvitrī wished to depart.

All the daughters of Dakṣa, beginning with Aditi, assembled;
surrounded by them, the virtuous Brahmāṇī whose abode is the lotus [departed].

One fair-faced woman took sweetmeats; another, taking a winnowing basket
filled with fruits, set out near Brahmā.

Others took pigeon peas along with niṣpāva beans; and another,
various pomegranates and beautiful citrons.

Others took karīra fruits and lotuses;
another took safflower, cumin, and dates.

Others carried excellent coconuts of all kinds;
one carried a vessel filled with grapes, and likewise water chestnuts.
Various kinds of camphor, auspicious rose-apples, / and walnuts, āmalakas, and lemons were brought by another,
and fully ripened bilva fruits, flattened rice, O lovely-faced one, / while others [brought] cotton rolls and safflower-dyed cloth.
Having placed these and other such things in a winnowing basket, the lovely-faced women, / all together with Sāvitrī, suddenly arrived, radiant.
Seeing Sāvitrī arrive, Indra was terrified there. / Brahmā stood with downcast face, [thinking,] "What will she say to me?"
Viṣṇu and Rudra were filled with shame, and so were all the other twice-born. / The members of the assembly were afraid, as were the other gods in heaven,
the sons, grandsons, nephews, maternal uncles, and brothers, / and the gods named Ṛbhus, deities even of the gods.
All stood in embarrassment, [wondering] what Sāvitrī would say. / But standing at Brahmā's side there was the cowherd girl,
observing silence, listening to the words spoken by everyone. / Though summoned by the adhvaryu priest, the fair-complexioned woman had not come.
Another woman had been brought by Indra from fear, given by Viṣṇu himself, / assented to by Rudra, and likewise given by her father.
"How will she act in the sacrifice, or how will it reach its completion?" / As they were thinking thus, the woman dwelling on a lotus entered.
Brahmā was surrounded by the assembly members, the officiating priests, and the gods, / and offerings were poured into the fires there by Brahmins who had mastered the Vedas.
The cowherd girl stood in the wife's pavilion, wearing an antelope horn and a girdle, / dressed in linen garments, meditating on the supreme abode,
devoted to her husband, holding her husband as her life, placed in the chief position, / endowed with beauty, large-eyed, resembling the sun in splendor,
illuminating that assembly just like the radiance of the sun. / Likewise, the officiating priests resorted to the blazing fire,
joyfully taking their respective share of the animals' sacrificial cake here. / The gods, desiring their share of the sacrifice, then said because of the delay:
"Nothing should be done out of season; what is done [too late] yields no fruit, / because such authority is seen in the Vedas by all the wise."
While the pravargya rite was being performed by the Brahmins who had mastered the Vedas, / combined with both kinds of milk boiled by the adhvaryu priest,
and when the twice-born had been invited and had come upon being summoned, / and the sacrificial food was being prepared, the goddess, seeing this, was filled with wrath.
The goddess said to Brahmā, who was silent in the midst of the assembly: / "Is it fitting, O god, to commit such a deed as this?
That, abandoning me out of desire, you have committed a sin! / She who is not equal even to the dust of my feet has been placed upon your head!
Whatever all these gathered people sitting in the assembly say, / carry out that command of the masters, if you so desire.
Out of greed for beauty, you have committed an act condemned by the world. / You felt no shame before your sons or before your grandsons, O Lord.
I consider this despised deed to have been done out of willful desire. / You are the grandfather of the gods, the great-grandfather of the sages.
How was no shame born in you as you looked upon your own person? / Mockery has been made in the midst of the world, and I have been wronged, O Lord.
If this is your firm intention, remain so, O god, homage to you! / How shall I show my face to my friends?
'A [second] wife was taken by my husband'—how can I say this?" / Brahmā said: / "I was urged by the officiating priests immediately after the time of initiation:
'Without a wife, no oblation can be made here; bring a wife here at once!' / She was brought by Indra, and this one was given to me by Viṣṇu,
and taken by me, O fair-browed one. Forgive this that has been done by me. / I shall never commit another offense against you, O woman of virtuous vows.
I have fallen at your feet; forgive me here, homage to you!" / Pulastya said: / Thus addressed, she became angry then and prepared to curse Brahmā:
"If I have performed penance, if my gurus have been satisfied, / in all assemblies of Brahmā and in various places,

The brāhmaṇas will never perform worship for you at all,
except for your single annual worship in the month of Kārttika.
and all the twice-born shall do it among mortals, nowhere else on earth!" / Having said this to Brahmā, she said to Indra who was present:
"Ho, Indra! You brought the cowherd woman near to Brahmā. / Since yours was a base deed, therefore you shall reap the fruit.
When you shall stand in the midst of battle, O Indra, / then, bound by your enemies, you will be reduced to the most dire state.
Destitute, your courage broken, dwelling in the city of your enemies, / having suffered great defeat, only after a long time will you be freed."
Having cursed Indra then, the goddess then addressed words to Viṣṇu: / "When, by the curse of Bhṛgu, your birth shall occur among mortals,
then you shall experience the sorrow born of separation from your wife there! / Your wife will be carried off by an enemy to the other shore of the great ocean,
and, your mind overwhelmed by grief, you will not know where she was taken. / Together with your brother, you will be miserable, having met with the most terrible calamity.
When you are born in the Yadu lineage and named Kṛṣṇa, / you will wander for a long time, reduced to servitude to cattle!"

Then, O Hara, when you were staying in the Dāruvana forest, angry at Rudra,
the enraged sages will bestow a curse on you, O Hara.
'Ho, base Kāpālika! You wish to take away our wives! / Therefore this arrogant phallus of yours shall fall to the earth today!'
Deprived of your virility and afflicted by the curse of the sages, / your wife, residing at Gaṅgādvāra, will console you.
O Agni, you were made an eater of everything formerly by my son, / by Bhṛgu, who is constant in dharma; how could I burn what is already burned?
O Jātavedas, that Rudra will flood you with his semen, / and in unholy things your tongue will burn even more."
Sāvitrī indeed cursed all the Brahmin officiating priests: / "Maintaining the agnihotra only for the sake of receiving gifts, living in vain in forests,
you shall always resort to sacred bathing-places and sacred sites purely out of greed! / Always satisfied by the food of others, but never satisfied in your own homes,
sacrificing for those for whom one should not sacrifice, accepting gifts from the contemptible, / earning wealth in vain, and expending it just as vainly!
Because of that, the state of hungry ghosts shall befall those ghosts; there is no doubt!" / Having thus in wrath cursed Indra, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Agni,
and Brahmā, and all those Brahmins as well, / having pronounced that curse upon them, she departed from the assembly.
Reaching senior Puṣkara, she then remained there. / She spoke to Lakṣmī, and to that chaste, fair-faced wife of Indra,
and to those young women she said: "I will not remain in this assembly; / and I shall go to that place where I will hear no sound."
Then all those women departed to their own abode. / Sāvitrī, enraged, was prepared to curse them as well:
"Since those wives of the gods have gone away, abandoning me, / I shall, being exceedingly enraged, give a curse to them as well!
Lakṣmī shall never have an abode in one place; / she shall be petty and fickle-minded, and shall dwell among fools,
among barbarians, mountain-dwellers, the vile and despised, / among fools, the arrogant, the accursed, and the wicked!"

"In such a manner, a human shall be your dwelling, caused by my curse."
Having thus cursed her, she then cursed Indrāṇī:
"When your husband Indra is seized by [the sin of] brahmahatyā and you share his grief, / Nahuṣa, having seized the kingdom, shall see you and desire you.
'I am Indra; how shall this foolish woman not attend upon me? / I shall slay all the gods if I do not obtain Śacī!'
Then, ruined, terrified, and grieving, in the house of the Lord of Speech / you shall dwell, you ill-behaved and arrogant woman, because of my curse!"

Then she pronounced a curse on all the wives of the gods:
"And all of you shall never obtain the joy that comes from having offspring!

Tormented day and night, defiled by the epithet 'barren woman'!"
In this manner, fair Gaurī too was then cursed by Sāvitrī.

Weeping, she was seen and propitiated by Viṣṇu:
"Do not weep, large-eyed one; come, arrive, O ever-auspicious lady!
Enter the assembly and grant me the girdle and the two linen garments; / accept the consecration, O consort of Brahmā, and I bow down at your feet!"
Thus addressed, she said to him: "I will not heed your word; / and I shall go to that place where I will hear no sound at all."

Having said this much, she climbed from that place and stood upon the mountain.
Viṣṇu, standing before her with his palms joined together,

bent low, stood full of supreme devotion, and praised her.
Viṣṇu said:
"You go everywhere; you are to be seen among all beings, wondrous on every side.

Whatever is visible, both real and unreal, does not exist without you.
Even so, the places in which you are to be seen by those seeking perfection,

or remembered by those desiring earthly prosperity, I shall declare in your presence:
[You are] named Sāvitrī at Puṣkara, the most excellent and auspicious of sacred bathing places;
Viśālākṣī at Vārāṇasī; Liṅgadhāriṇī at Naimiṣa; / the goddess Lalitā at Prayāga; Kāmukā on the Gandhamādana mountain;
named Kumudā at Mānasa; Viśvakāyā in the atmosphere; / named Gomatī on the Gomanta mountain; Kāmacāriṇī on the Mandara mountain;
Madotkaṭā in Caitraratha; Jayantī at Hastināpura; / likewise Gaurī at Kānyakubja; Rambhā on the Malaya mountain;
Kīrtimatī at Ekāmraka; Viśvā and Viśveśvarī [there]; / Puruhastā at Karṇikā; Mārgadāyikā at Kedāra;
Nandā on the back of the Himavat; Bhadrakālikā at Gokarṇa; / Bhavānī at Sthāṇvīśvara; Bilvapatrikā at Bilvaka;
the goddess Mādhavī at Śrīśaila; Bhadrā and Bhadreśvarī; / Jayā on the Varāha mountain; Kamalā at Kamalālaya;
Rudrāṇī at Rudrakoṭi; Kālī at Kālañjara; / Kapilā at Mahāliṅga; Maṅgaleśvarī at Karkoṭa;
Mahādevī at Śālagrāma; Jalapriyā at Śivaliṅga; / Kumārī at Māyāpurī; Lalitā in the Saṃtāna grove;
Utpalākṣī at Sahasrākṣa; Mahotpalā at Hiraṇyākṣa; / named Maṅgalā at Gayā; Vimalā at Puruṣottama;
Amoghākṣī on the Vipāśā; Pāṭalā at Puṇyavardhana; / Nārāyaṇī at Supārśva; Bhadrasundarī on Trikūṭa;
named Vipulā on Vipula; Kalyāṇī on the Malaya mountain; / Koṭavī at Koṭitīrtha; Sugandhā in the Mādhavī grove;
Trisandhyā at Kubjāmraka; Haripriyā at Gaṅgādvāra; / Śivānandā at Śivakuṇḍa; Nandinī on the bank of the Devikā;
Rukmiṇī at Dvāravatī; Rādhā in Vṛndāvana; / Devakī at Mathurā; Parameśvarī in the netherworld;
Sītā at Citrakūṭa; Vindhyanivāsinī in the Vindhya mountains; / Ekavīrā on the Sahya mountain; Candrikā at Hariścandra;
Ramaṇā at Rāmatīrtha; Mṛgāvatī on the Yamunā; / Mahālakṣmī at Karavīra; the goddess Umā at Vināyaka;
Arogā at Vaidyanātha; Maheśvarī at Mahākāla; / Abhayā at Puṣpatīrtha; Amṛtā in the cave of the Vindhya mountain;
the goddess Māṇḍavī at Māṇḍavya; Svāhā in the city of Māheśvara; / Pracaṇḍā at Vegalā; and Caṇḍikā at Amarakaṇṭaka;
Varārohā at Someśvara; Puṣkarāvatī at Prabhāsa; / Devamātā on the Sarasvatī; residing on the shore of the vast sea;
Mahāpadmā at Mahālaya; Piṅgaleśvarī on the Payoṣṇī; / Siṃhikā at Kṛtaśauca; Śaṅkarī at Kārtikeya;
Lolā at Utpalāvartaka; Subhadrā at the confluence of the Sindhu; / Umā in the Siddha forest; Lakṣmī-Anaṅgā at Bharata's hermitage;
Viśvamukhī at Jālandhara; Tārā on the Kiṣkindha mountain; / Puṣṭi in the Devadāru forest; Medhā in the realm of Kaśmīra;
the goddess Bhīmā on the Himādri; Tuṣṭi at Vastreśvara; / Śraddhā at Kapālamocana; Mātā at Kāyāvarohaṇa;
named Dhvani at Śaṅkhoddhāra; Dhṛti at Piṇḍāraka; / Kālā on the Candrabhāgā; Siddhidayinī at Acchoda;
the goddess Amṛtā on the Veṇā; Urvaśī at Badarī; / Auṣadhī in Uttarakuru; Kuśodakā in Kuśadvīpa;
Manmathā on Hemakūṭa; Satyavādinī on Kumuda; / Vandanīyā in the sacred fig tree; Nidhi in the abode of Vaiśravaṇa;
Gāyatrī in the mouth of the Veda; Pārvatī in the presence of Śiva; / Indrāṇī in the world of the gods; Sarasvatī in the mouth of Brahmā;
named Prabhā in the orb of the sun; Vaiṣṇavī among the mothers; / Arundhatī among chaste wives; Tilottamā among beautiful women;

named Brahmakalā in the mind; the power of all embodied beings.
This excellent [hymn of] one hundred and eight names has been proclaimed by me with devotion,

and this one hundred and eight sacred bathing places has been declared.
Whoever recites it or even hears it is freed from all sins.

Whatever best of men, having bathed in these sacred bathing places, should see [her],
freed from all sins, shall dwell in the city of Brahmā for an eon.
A man who causes these one hundred and eight names to be heard in the presence of Brahmā / on the full moon or on the new moon day shall have many sons.
At the donation of a cow, or at the presentation of a śrāddha, or day after day / during the rite of worshipping the gods, hearing it, he attains the supreme Brahman.

To Viṣṇu who was praising her thus, Sāvitrī of virtuous vows said:
"I have been properly praised by you, son; you shall be invincible.

In your incarnations, you shall have a wife and be dear to your father and mother.
And whoever, having come here, praises me with this hymn,

freed from all sins, shall go to the supreme abode.
Go, bring the sacrifice of Viriñci to completion, my son!

At Kurukṣetra and at Prayāga, I shall become the bestower of food.
Standing near my husband, I will fulfill your word."

Thus addressed, Viṣṇu went to the excellent assembly of Brahmā.
Now, when Sāvitrī had departed, Gāyatrī spoke these words:

"Let the sages hear my word in the presence of my husband,
which I, being pleased, declare, ready to grant a boon:
Those men who worship Brahmā endowed with devotion, / to them will belong clothing, wealth, grain, wives, happiness, and riches.
Likewise, unbroken happiness in the household with sons and grandsons; / having enjoyed this for a very long time, in the end he will attain liberation."

Pulastya said:
Having installed [an image of] Brahmā with every effort according to the ritual rules, / the meritorious fruit that one attains—listen to that with a one-pointed mind.
Whatever fruit is obtained in all sacrifices, austerities, gifts, sacred places, and Vedas, / that fruit multiplied ten million times one would obtain through this installation.
Having observed a fast on the full moon day with devotion, O lord of men, / whatever man worships Viriñci according to this ritual,
on the first day of the lunar fortnight, O mighty-armed one, goes to the abode of Brahmā; / [worshipping] Viriñci and Vāsudeva, especially through the officiating priests.
In the month of Kārttika, the chariot procession of the god is proclaimed, / having performed which with devotion, human beings attain the world of Brahmā.
In the month of Kārttika, on the full moon day, O king of kings, O tormentor of enemies, [one should lead] the four-faced Brahmā, along with Sāvitrī,
accompanied by various musical instruments, through the entire city. / Having led him around, O king, one should bathe the world-protector and the city.
Having first fed the brāhmaṇas and worshipped Śāṇḍileya, / one should mount the god on the chariot amid the sounds of auspicious musical instruments.
Having worshipped the son of Śāṇḍilī in front of the chariot according to rule, / having the brāhmaṇas recite blessings and performing the auspicious ceremony of the auspicious day,
and having mounted the god on the chariot, one should keep vigil / with various kinds of spectacles and abundant recitations of the sacred text.
Having kept vigil for the god, in the morning, O king, / having fed the brāhmaṇas according to one's ability with manifold chewable and solid foods,
and having worshipped the steadfast people with mantra[s] according to rule, O king, / with clarified butter, O mighty-armed one, with milk, and with milk-rice,
having caused the brāhmaṇas to recite blessings according to rule, O king, / and having proclaimed the word 'auspicious day', one should lead that chariot around the city.
One should have Brahmā's chariot drawn by brāhmaṇas learned in the four Vedas— / by Rigvedins, Atharvavedins, O hero, and likewise by Sāmavedins and Yajurvedins.
One should lead that chariot of the god of gods, the best of deities, / clockwise around the entire city along a very smooth path.
The chariot must not be drawn, O hero, by a śūdra desiring welfare; / nor should a wise king climb into the chariot, except for a single priest.
On the right side of Brahmā, O king, one should place Gāyatrī; / on the left side, the priest; and in front, one should place a lotus.
Thus, with sounds of horns and abundant blasts of conches, / having led the chariot, O hero, clockwise around the entire city,
the wise person should reinstall the god in his own place after offering a waving of lamps. / Whoever performs this procession thus, or even gazes upon it with devotion,
or pulls the chariot, goes to the abode of Brahmā. / And whoever performs the lighting of lamps on the new-moon day in the month of Kārttika
in the hall of Brahmā, goes to the supreme abode. / But whoever honors himself with perfumes, flowers, and new garments
on that first lunar day, goes to the abode of Brahmā. / This lunar day is most meritorious, inaugurating the reign of Bali.
It is eternally very dear to Brahmā, proclaimed as Bali's day. / Whoever worships Brahmā on this [day], and especially himself,
goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu of immeasurable splendor. / In the month of Caitra, O mighty-armed one, the first lunar day is the best and meritorious.
On that [day], the best among men who bathes after touching an outcaste / has no misfortune whatsoever, nor mental anguish, nor diseases, O king.
They do not occur, O tiger of the Kurus; therefore one should perform that bath. / For that divine waving of lamps destroys all diseases.
Whatever there is of cows, buffaloes, and so forth, O king, one should cause all that to run; / by means of all that, along with garments and other things, one should erect an archway outside.
Likewise, one should provide food for brāhmaṇas, O upholder of the Kuru lineage. / For these three lunar days were declared of old, O joy of the Kurus:
in the month of Kārttika, in Āśvina, and likewise in the month of Caitra, O king. / Bathing and giving on the lunar day sacred to Kārttikeya [bear] a hundredfold fruit, O king;
and the [day] of King Bali brings auspiciousness and benefits cattle. / Gāyatrī said: / 'The statement that was spoken by that Sāvitrī to the lotus-born [Brahmā]—
"Brāhmaṇas will never perform worship to you"— / yet those who, hearing my words, perform worship [to you],
having enjoyed pleasures here, will be partakers of liberation in the hereafter.' / Knowing this supreme vision, pleased, she grants a boon:
'O Śakra, I shall grant you a boon for victory in battle and suppression of enemies; / then Brahmā, having gone to the abode of the enemy, will deliver [you].
You will regain your lost city and, from the destruction of the enemy, supreme joy; / an uncontested, great sovereignty will be yours in the three worlds.
When, O Viṣṇu, you make an incarnation in the mortal world, / [experiencing] supreme suffering along with your brother arising from the abduction of your wife,
having slain the enemy, you will regain your wife in the presence of the gods; / having received her and having ruled again, you will go to heaven.
For eleven thousand years [you will rule] and then [return to] heaven; / your renown will be vast in the world, along with affection from the people.
The worlds of those [people] belonging to your line will endure, purified; / those mortals will be carried across by you, O god, in the form of Rāma.'
Gāyatrī then, granting boons, addressed Rudra: / 'Even if your liṅga has fallen, those people who worship it,
purified and of meritorious deeds, are partakers of the heavenly world. / Not by the agnihotra, nor by a sacrifice offered into the fire, [does one attain]
that goal which human beings reach from the worship of your liṅga. / Those who always on the bank of the Gaṅgā worship your liṅga with bilva leaves
early in the morning will be partakers of Rudra's world. / Even after attaining devotion to Śarva, O Agni, be you the purifier!
When you are pleased, all the gods are indeed pleased—there is no doubt of this. / Through your mouth the oblations are enjoyed by the gods; when you are pleased, they are surely pleased,
they eat [them]—there is no doubt of this, just as stated in the Veda.' / Gāyatrī said this to those brāhmaṇas, every one of them:
'Having propitiated you at all sacred bathing places, mortals / will all go, without doubt, to the realm called Vairāja.
Having offered various kinds of food and manifold gifts, / and having pleased [you] in ancestral rites, they become gods of gods.
And in the mouths of those who are the best among brāhmaṇas, the dwellers of heaven / swiftly eat the oblation to the gods, and the ancestors [eat] the offering to the ancestors.
For you are capable of sustaining the three worlds, there is no doubt; / and by a single breath-control you will all become purified.
Especially after bathing at Puṣkara and reciting me, the mother of the Vedas, / you will not incur the faults incurred from accepting gifts, O best of the twice-born.
And by the gift of food at Puṣkara, all deities will be pleased; / when a single brāhmaṇa is fed, the fruit of ten million [fed] will be obtained.
Sins such as killing a brāhmaṇa and evil deeds that have been committed— / all men will [efface them] by placing wealth in your hands.
When [Brahmā] is worshipped through my recitation performed three times, / a sin equal to killing a brāhmaṇa is destroyed at that very instant.
A sin accrued over ten births, or done of old over a hundred, / or over three ages, or over a thousand, Gāyatrī destroys.
Knowing thus, you will constantly be purified through the recitation of my [mantra], / there is no doubt; no hesitation should be entertained here.
Especially having recited [it] with the three-measure Praṇava / along with the head, all will be purified, there is no doubt.
I exist consisting of eight syllables, and this universe is pervaded by me; / I am the mother of all the Vedas, adorned with all [sacred] lines.
Having recited me with devotion, the best of the twice-born will attain perfection; / pre-eminence will belong to all of you through the recitation of my [mantra].
Even a brāhmaṇa possessing only the Gāyatrī as his essence, who is well-restrained, is preferable; / not an unrestrained master of the four Vedas who eats everything and sells everything.'
Because a curse was laid upon the Brahmins by Sāvitrī in the assembly, / whatever is given or offered into the fire here shall become imperishable.
Therefore a boon has been granted by me to you, O best of the twice-born: / Brahmins devoted to the agnihotra, offering oblations at the three twilights,
shall go to heaven along with twenty-one generations of their families. / Thus to Śakra, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Agni,
to Brahmā and to the Brahmins, Gāyatrī granted the supreme boon / at that very Puṣkara, and then stood beside Brahmā.
The cause of the curse of Lakṣmī was then narrated by the bards; / and knowing the curses laid upon all the young women individually,
Gāyatrī, the beloved of Brahmā, also granted a boon to Lakṣmī: / "Ever making all men uncensured, splendid with wealth,
you shall shine without doubt, bestowing delight upon all. / Those who are looked upon by you, daughter, shall all enjoy holy merits;
whereas those who are forsaken by you shall all share in misery. / Their birth, family, character, and virtue, O fair-faced one,
shall shine in the assembly, and they shall be looked upon by kings; / and the best of the twice-born shall indeed make supplication to them.
They show gentleness to them, [saying:] 'You are our brother, father, and teacher, / and a kinsman without doubt; I cannot live without you.
When you are seen, my gaze becomes bright and gracious; / my mind is exceedingly pleased: truly, truly I say this to you.'
Such words those good men who are regarded with your gaze / will hear, bringing delight to the people.
Attaining the status of Indra and seeing you, Nahuṣa will make a petition; / but smitten by your glance, that sinful one will surely [fall] by Agastya's word.
Arriving at the state of a serpent, he will implore him: / 'I am ruined through pride; be my refuge, O sage!'
At that word of that king, the revered sage, / bringing compassion into his mind, will speak these words:
'A king, the delight of his race, will be born in your lineage; / seeing you bearing the form of a serpent, he will shatter your curse.
Then, abandoning serpenthood, you will go once more to heaven.' / Together with your husband who has performed the horse sacrifice, to heaven again
you shall attain through this granting of my boon, O fair-eyed one." / Pulastya said: / Then all the wives of the gods were addressed by that contented lady:
"Even though devoid of offspring, you shall not suffer any sorrow." / And Gaurī too was then instructed by Gāyatrī.
Enriched with satisfaction, having granted boons, that wise lady, / the beloved of Brahmā, was eager for the completion of his sacrifice.
Seeing Gāyatrī, the mother of the Vedas, thus granting boons, / Rudra then bowed down and uttered this praise:
Rudra said: / "Homage to you, O Mother of the Vedas, purified by the eight syllables, / Gāyatrī, savior from misfortune, and sevenfold speech!
All the treatises of praise, all the meters, / all the syllables, and likewise all the grammatical rules,
all the treatises beginning with commentaries, and whatever other rules there are, / and all the letters of the alphabet—you indeed are they, O goddess; homage to you!
You are white, white of form, with a face resembling the moon, / bearing large arms tender as the core of a plantain tree,
holding a deer horn and an immaculate lotus in your hand, / dressed in two linen garments, with a red upper cloth,
splendid upon your chest with a necklace shining like the rays of the moon, / beautifully adorned with ears filled with divine earrings,
you shine with a face that rivals the moon, / adorned with a most pure diadem and braided hair!
Your two arms, resembling coils of serpents, are an ornament of heaven; / your breasts, O goddess, are radiant, round, and with even nipples;
proud with the curve of the three folds of skin above a very fair hip; / situated in the center is your navel, deep and auspicious to behold;
a goddess with wide hips, beautifully proportioned, O fair-faced one, / with a pair of well-formed, round thighs, and excellent knees and feet!
As the bearer of the three worlds, you whose petitions are true / will become on earth the grantor of boons, O highly fortunate and fair-complexioned one!
And the pilgrimage made to Puṣkara will be accomplished upon beholding you; / on the full moon day in the month of Jyeṣṭha, you will receive the foremost worship.
And whatever men, knowing your power, shall worship you, / nothing will be difficult for them to attain, whether in sons or in wealth.
For those sunken in wildernesses, in a forest, or on the great ocean, / or surrounded by bandits, you are the supreme refuge of men.
You are accomplishment, fortune, steadfastness, renown, modesty, knowledge, humility, and intellect; / you are twilight, night, dawn, sleep, and Kālarātri herself.
You are the mother, Kamalā, the mother [of all], Brahmāṇī, the celibate student, / the mother of all the gods, Gāyatrī, the supreme woman,
Jayā and Vijayā, nourishment, forbearance, and compassion; / you are the younger sister of Sāvitrī, and ever dear to the Grandfather.
Multiform, universal in form, fair-eyed, celibate, / of beautiful form, large-eyed, the protectress of devotees!
In sacred cities and in hermitages, O fair-faced one, / in forests and groves is your dwelling, O great goddess!
In all the places of Brahmā, you stand to the left of Brahmā; / to the right is Sāvitrī, and in the middle stands Brahmā the Grandfather.
You are the inner altar of sacrifices and the sacrificial fee of the priests; / you are indeed the success of kings, and considered the shoreline born of the ocean.
You are the initiation of the celibate student, and regarded as supreme beauty; / you are the radiance of the luminaries, O goddess, and Lakṣmī residing in Nārāyaṇa.
You are forbearance and the accomplishment of sages, and Rohiṇī among the lunar mansions; / at royal gates, at holy bathing places, and at the confluences of rivers,
on the full moon and in the full moon, in intellect, in policy, forbearance, and resolution, / and as the goddess Umā among women, you are celebrated, O fair-complexioned one!

You are the lovely gaze of Indra, abiding in his thousand eyes;
you are the sense of righteousness of the sages, and the supreme refuge of the gods.
You are the furrow for farmers, and the earth for living beings; / you prevent widowhood for women, and ever bestow wealth and grain.
When worshipped, you will quell sickness, death, and fear; / likewise, when well worshipped on the full moon day in the month of Kārttika,
you will be the goddess who grants all desires, O giver of auspiciousness! / And whatever man recites or constantly listens to this hymn,
